We're actually not far from peak ICE efficiency which can fit in a vehicle. Average gas engine gets roughly 25% efficiency and a diesel gets roughly 30% efficiency. That remaining 70%-75% loss is basically wasted heat. Which we then add more weight and complexity to mitigate (radiator and water pump). Basically the only way you're going to improve upon that is one of the followings: different material (steel instead of cast iron/aluminum), higher compression rates, larger scales.

Steel engines are much more expensive and generally heavier. So while thermal efficiency may increase the total work required for break-even from the change is also higher. Higher compression requires better fuels and more complex engine designs. Maintenance also becomes more important. Even here, there limits are very real. Which leaves us with scale.

Scale is actually one of the primary reasons that electric vehicles are more efficient than ICE. Because they get their electricity from sources were already benefit from economy of scale. While a diesel truck may be running around with 30% efficiency, a large diesel generator can something something in the 50%-60% range. Which I believe is approaching theoretical limits for ICE.

Electric vehicles get a little more complex in measuring efficiency because of so many variants. But direct drive electric cars can have roughly 95% efficiency to the road. Whereas your typical ICE sees around 15%, after your vehicle actually moves. But... most electric vehicles are not direct drive. They tend to still go through a transmission of some type or use various regenerative systems which further complicates things. Regardless, when you combine electric motor efficiency with economy of scale efficiency (which can include nuclear), and power distribution, electric vehicles tend to be much more efficient.

Like it or not electric vehicles are the way of the future. Some day anyways. Power pack energy density remains the biggest challenge for the foreseeable future. The second challenge is cost. Electric vehicles are more expensive. The combination of cost and range makes it difficult to compete head to head. But since most drivers don't drive long trip distances 80% of non-commercial driving in the US can be filled by electric vehicles today.
